questions.q: Why does the `require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount, ...)` check need to run before any balance is changed?
options: require only works if it's the last line of the function
It doesn't actually matter what order it runs in
To make the function cost less gas overall
So the entire transaction reverts immediately if funds are insufficient, before any state change happens
questions.explain: Checking first means an insufficient-funds transaction reverts before any balances are touched — protecting against ending up in an inconsistent, partially-updated state.

questions.q: In the real transfer function, what happens to the sender's and receiver's balances?
options: Only the receiver's balance changes
Balances are unaffected — only the event fires
Both balances increase by amount
The sender's balance decreases by amount, and the receiver's increases by amount
questions.explain: balances[msg.sender] -= amount removes the amount from the sender, and balances[to] += amount adds it to the receiver.

questions.q: Why are both `from` and `to` marked `indexed` in the Transfer event?
options: It makes the event emit for free
Indexed parameters are required for the event to compile at all
So the event can be searched either by sender or by receiver
Only one address can ever be indexed at a time
questions.explain: Indexing both from and to lets a block explorer or front end filter transfers by either the sending address or the receiving address.

questions.q: What real, standard order of operations does this function follow?
options: emit, then mutate state, then require
There is no consistent order — it's arbitrary
mutate state, then require, then emit
require, then mutate state, then emit
questions.explain: The function checks its condition first (require), only then changes balances (mutate), and finally announces the change (emit) — the standard real order.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is this simple transfer function described as "the core of what an ERC-20 token contract does"?
options: It combines a balances mapping, a require guard, state-changing arithmetic, and an event — the same real building blocks a full token contract extends
This function is only used for testing and never appears in production
It has no real connection to actual token standards
ERC-20 tokens never use mappings or events
questions.explain: Every concept from this chapter — mappings, require guards, mapping arithmetic, and events — appears together in this one function, which is genuinely the same shape real ERC-20 contracts build on.
